hints: Picking greedily on the way there can ruin the way back. Instead, think of the return trip reversed — it becomes a second walk from the top-left going right/down. What if both walkers move at the same time?

3D DP with two walkers moving together: after t steps walker A is at (r1, t−r1) and walker B at (r2, t−r2). The state (t, r1, r2) stores the most berries; if both stand on the same cell, count its berry once.

1. dp[r1][r2] for the current step t, start with dp[0][0] = field[0][0].
  2. For t = 1..2n−2: for each r1, r2 with valid columns c1 = t−r1, c2 = t−r2 and no rocks:
  3. best = max of the 4 previous states (each walker came from up or left).
  4. Gain = field[r1][c1] + (same cell ? 0 : field[r2][c2]); new dp = best + gain.
  5. Answer = max(0, dp[n−1][n−1]) at the last step (unreachable → 0).

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Enumerate every path there and every path back, and count berries for each pair.

approaches.name: Wrong greedy
approaches.idea: Take the best path there, clear its berries, then the best path back. This can miss the optimum, so it is not correct.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Two simultaneous walkers, DP over (step, row1, row2).

explain: In sample 1 the walkers can take different routes around the rock in the middle: one goes along the top and right edge, the other along the left and bottom edge, picking all 6 berries. Moving both walkers in lockstep is the key: they share a cell only when they are on it at the same step, so 'pick once' is easy to enforce. Rocks and out-of-range cells get −infinity. If the exit cannot be reached (sample 2 is blocked by rocks), the final value is −infinity and we return 0.
recognize: Go there and come back on a grid collecting items only once → model as two walkers moving together, DP over (step, row1, row2).
